card.name: Ohafia War Dance
card.tagline: A traditional Igbo war dance from Nigeria commemorating historical martial prowess.
card.profile: The Ohafia War Dance, known in Igbo as ikpirikpi ogu, is a traditional performance originating from the Ohafia region of Eastern Nigeria. It serves as a commemoration of the strength and martial history of the Ohafia people, who were historically renowned as warriors. The dance is performed by men who mimic the actions of battle, including the ritualistic beheading of enemies, to celebrate both collective history and individual achievements.
card.insight: The lead dancer of the Ohafia War Dance carries a basket of human skulls, known as oyaya, while holding a cutlass and a palm shoot in his mouth to signify the warrior heritage of the Ohafia people.

card.profile_long:
The Ohafia War Dance, or ikpirikpi ogu, is a significant cultural performance rooted in the history of the Ohafia people of Eastern Nigeria. Historically, the Ohafia ancestors were recognized as mighty men of war, and their warrior tradition remains a fundamental aspect of their identity. This identity is deeply connected to the practice of ikpirikpi ogu, which historically involved the beheading of a fallen enemy as proof of a man's courage and strength. 

In the past, this martial requirement was the gateway to the Ogbu-Isi society. Only those who successfully brought home a human head were permitted to join this society and wear an eagle's plume, which served as a visible symbol of their bravery. Today, the dance is performed by a group of muscular men to commemorate the strength and success of their ancestors in past wars. 

The performance is structured around a lead dancer who carries a basket full of human skulls, referred to as oyaya. This lead dancer also carries a short cutlass and holds a small palm shoot in his mouth. Surrounding him, fellow dancers are dressed as fierce warriors. These dancers perform movements that mime the act of cutting off human heads, effectively portraying Ohafia as a land of brave warriors. The performance is accompanied by music played on the akwatankwa instrument. Beyond its historical roots, the dance is also utilized to celebrate the achievements of individuals within the community. Due to the limited available documentation, specific details regarding the choreography, footwork, and musical structure remain largely unrecorded in current sources.

claims.text: The Ohafia War Dance (Igbo: ikpirikpi ogu) is a popular war dance performed in several parts of Eastern Nigeria.
The Ohafia warrior tradition which remains one of the fundamental identity of the people of Ohafia is hinged in the performance of ikpirikpi ogu - the practice of beheading a fallen enemy.
Only those who brought home a human head could join the Ogbu-Isi society and wear an eagle's plume which is a symbol of courage.
The dance which has its roots from Ohafia is performed by a group of muscular men in commemoration of their strength in fighting and winning wars in the past.
The Ohafia War Dance which is also performed to celebrate an individual's achievement is headed by a lead dancer carrying a basket full of human skulls (Igbo: oyaya).
Fellow dancers dressed like fierce warriors mime the cutting off of human head while dancing to the music from the akwatankwa musical instrument.
